definition: How much a spacecraft can change its speed with the fuel it carries. Every manoeuvre, such as braking into orbit around the Moon, costs some Δv.
How efficiently an engine uses fuel. Higher Isp means more Δv from the same amount of propellant.
An orbit a few hundred kilometres up. Close, cheap to reach and easy to talk to, but with frequent passes through Earth's shadow.
A polar orbit that passes over each place at the same local time every day, so lighting stays consistent between images.
An orbit 35,786 km above the equator where a satellite turns with the Earth and seems to hover over one spot.
The part of an orbit spent in a planet's or moon's shadow. Solar panels produce nothing, so batteries must take over.
Spare capacity kept on purpose, such as extra power or mass the design does not use yet. Engineers keep margins because estimates grow as designs mature.
The spacecraft's body: structure, wiring and basic systems that carry and support the instruments.
The equipment a mission exists for, usually the science instruments.
Sending data from the spacecraft to antennas on Earth. Limited by distance, antenna size, transmitter power and contact time.
How much stronger a radio link is than the minimum needed, measured in decibels (dB). 3 dB means twice the minimum.
Onboard storage that holds science data until the next ground-station contact. If it fills up, new data is lost.
Electronics built to survive energetic particles from the Sun and deep space without errors or damage.
The chance a part keeps working for a year. Spacecraft reliability is the product of all its parts, so weak parts matter.
A time-ordered description of what the mission does, from launch to end of life.
A table linking each science goal to the measurement it needs, the instrument that makes it and the requirement that checks it.
The list of every part on the spacecraft with its mass, power and cost.
Baseline is the science return for full success. Threshold is the minimum that still counts as partial success.
A JPL scale for how developed a mission idea is, from a sketch (CML 1) to a point design (CML 4). GRAVITY's difficulty levels follow it.
The window of days in which a launch must happen to reach the target. Missing it can mean waiting months or years.
